programs.nl_rule:
In the input, you should see...a unicolored background containing a few same-colored, three-cell L-shaped objects. Each object occupies three of the four cells of a 2×2 square.

The output grid size...is the same as the input grid size.

To make the output, you have to...for each L-shaped object, identify the missing fourth cell of its 2×2 square. The diagonal direction from the L's elbow cell toward this missing cell determines the direction in which the object points. Leave the missing cell empty, but continue one step farther in the same diagonal direction and start a line there. Extend this diagonal line, in the same color as the object, until it reaches the edge of the grid. Repeat this independently for every L-shaped object.

content.text:
Let me understand the rule and the verifier.

The verifier: objects are extracted with univalued=T, diagonal=F, without_bg=T. So each connected component (4-connectivity) of same-colored non-background cells.

There are several filters:
- x19: objects where toindices == toindices - lrcorner, i.e., lrcorner is NOT in the object? Wait, sfilter keeps elements satisfying condition. x18 = fork(equality, toindices, x17) where x17 = fork(remove, lrcorner, toindices). So x17(obj) = toindices(obj) with lrcorner removed. x18 checks toindices == toindices with lrcorner removed, meaning lrcorner is not in toindices... wait equality of full set with set-minus-lrcorner is true only if lrcorner not in the set. Hmm, that's weird for L-shapes.

Wait actually toindices returns the set of indices. remove(lrcorner, toindices) removes lrcorner from set. equality(set, set\{lrcorner}) is True iff lrcorner not in set. But lrcorner is min/max... lrcorner of a patch is (max i, max j). For an L-shape missing a corner... hmm.

Wait, let me reconsider. Actually these filters seem odd. Let's re-read.

x17 = fork(remove, lrcorner, toindices): remove(value, container). fork applies outer(remove) to a=lrcorner? No: fork(outer, a, b) = lambda x: outer(a(x), b(x)). So x17 = lambda x: remove(lrcorner(x), toindices(x)). Yes removes lrcorner.

x18 = equality(toindices(x), x17(x)). True iff lrcorner(x) not in toindices(x). But lrcorner(x) is by definition an element of the patch's indices (well, computed from indices). Hmm, toindices... for an Object (frozenset of (value, index) pairs) toindices returns the indices. lrcorner computes from patch. So lrcorner is always in the set. So equality would be False always?? That can't be.

Wait, unless lrcorner computes over the object differently... ulcorner uses toindices(patch). lrcorner also uses toindices. So lrcorner always in set. So filter x19 keeps nothing.

Hmm wait let me re-read: maybe I mis-assigned. Let me recheck urcorner etc.

Actually wait: sfilter keeps elements where condition is True. If condition always False, then x19 etc are empty. That would make x29 etc empty. Then output would just be input. But example output has changes. So I must be misreading.

Hmm, wait. Let me reconsider fork(remove, lrcorner, toindices). outer=remove, a=lrcorner, b=toindices. remove(lrcorner(x), toindices(x)). Yes.

Hmm. Unless `toindices` for object returns indices, and lrcorner returns... there might be a subtlety. Actually maybe the intended filter is opposite: keep objects where removing the corner changes the set... no.

Hold on, let me reconsider. Maybe these are meant to detect which corner is missing. For an L-shape (3 cells of 2x2), the object's bounding box is 2x2, but one cell missing. The corners of the object's own indices: for an L occupying e.g. cells (0,0),(0,1),(1,0) [missing (1,1) bottom-right], the computed lrcorner = (max i, max j) = (1,1). But (1,1) is not in the set! lrcorner computes tuple(map(max, zip(*toindices))). For this set, max i=1, max j=1 → (1,1). Indeed lrcorner is (1,1) which is NOT in the set. 

So remove(lrcorner, toindices) = toindices unchanged, equality True. Good, so x19 keeps objects where lrcorner (max,max) is not in the set → the object is missing its bottom-right corner. Then x3 = chain(x1, x2, lrcorner): x1=shoot with UNITY, x2=add UNITY, lrcorner. So x3(obj) = shoot(add(lrcorner(obj), UNITY), UNITY) = shoot(lrcorner + (1,1), (1,1)). lrcorner + UNITY = (max+1, max+1), the missing cell position. Then shoot from there in direction (1,1) downward-right to edge. recolor with object's color. So the line starts at the missing cell (the diagonal one step from elbow toward the missing corner) and extends to the edge. 

Wait, the rule says "Leave the missing cell empty, but continue one step farther in the same diagonal direction and start a line there." Let's check: the missing cell is at lrcorner+UNITY = (1,1) for that object. But shoot starts at add(lrcorner, UNITY) = the missing cell itself, not one step farther. Hmm.

Wait let's recheck: x3 = chain(x1, x2, lrcorner) = x1(x2(lrcorner(obj))) = shoot(add(lrcorner(obj), UNITY), UNITY). So start = lrcorner + (1,1). For object missing bottom-right, lrcorner=(1,1) computed, missing cell is (1,1) itself. So start = (2,2). Hmm, lrcorner is (1,1), add UNITY = (2,2). So start is (2,2) which is one step beyond the missing cell (1,1) in direction (1,1). Yes! Because lrcorner computed = (max i, max j) = (1,1) = missing cell position. add UNITY gives (2,2), one farther. 

Wait but the rule says "Leave the missing cell empty, but continue one step farther in the same diagonal direction and start a line there." The missing cell is (1,1). One step farther is (2,2). Yes matches.

Actually wait: is the missing cell at (max+... ). For object with cells (0,0),(0,1),(1,0), missing is (1,1) = lrcorner computed. Yes since lrcorner = (max,max) = (1,1). Good.

Now for the example: first object: cells at (2,7),(3,7),(3,8). Let's see: row2 col7=6, row3 col7=6, row3 col8=6. That's an L: (2,7),(3,7),(3,8). Missing corner: the 2x2 square rows2-3, cols7-8. Occupied: (2,7),(3,7),(3,8). Missing (2,8). So it's missing top-right corner. Elbow is (3,7) (the cell adjacent to both others). Diagonal direction from elbow (3,7) toward missing (2,8) is up-right = (-1,+1). Output should have a line starting one step beyond missing cell (2,8) → (1,9) going up-right: (1,9), then (0,10) out of bounds. So output line: (1,9)=6. Indeed output row1 col9=6. Yes matches!

Second object: cells (7,2),(8,1),(8,2). 2x2 square rows7-8, cols1-2. Occupied: (7,2),(8,1),(8,2). Missing (7,1) top-left. Elbow (8,2). Direction from elbow toward missing: (-1,-1) up-left. Missing cell (7,1); one step farther (6,0). Line from (6,0) going up-left: (6,0),(5,-1) out. So output (6,0)=6. Indeed output row6 col0=6. 

Now which filter handles this object? Missing top-left → ulcorner not in set. x25 = filter where ulcorner not in set. x12 = chain with ulcorner using NEG_UNITY: x12 = shoot(add(ulcorner, NEG_UNITY), NEG_UNITY). ulcorner = (min i, min j) = (7,1) = missing cell. add NEG_UNITY = (6,0) one step. shoot up-left. 

So the filters and mapping:
- lrcorner missing (bottom-right) → shoot direction UNITY (down-right), from lrcorner+UNITY.
- urcorner missing (top-right) → x8: shoot UP_RIGHT (-1,1), from urcorner+UP_RIGHT.
- ulcorner missing (top-left) → shoot NEG_UNITY (-1,-1), from ulcorner+NEG_UNITY.
- llcorner missing (bottom-left) → shoot DOWN_LEFT (1,-1), from llcorner+DOWN_LEFT.

So basically for each L object, the missing corner is the "far corner" in the diagonal pointing direction; line starts one step beyond missing corner, extends to edge, in object color, missing cell stays empty.

Wait, but note: the line starts at one step beyond the missing cell, so the missing cell remains empty (as rule says). Good.

Now I need to teach the student. Since it's a symmetric simple rule, I can show examples via show_example or show_transformed_input. The verifier is the real thing. Best to show_transformed_input with a few inputs covering all four orientations. Since the environment fills gold output, that's reliable. Let me give multiple inputs.

Actually a single input can contain all four orientations. Let me construct one input with four L-shapes, each missing a different corner, placed so lines don't overlap confusingly (though overlaps of same color don't matter). Use a background 0 and color e.g. 3.

Let me design a grid, say 12x12.

Objects (color 6):
Orientation A: missing bottom-right (elbow is top-left). Cells: (r,c),(r,c+1),(r+1,c). E.g. at r=1,c=1: cells (1,1),(1,2),(2,1). Missing (2,2). Line from (3,3) direction (1,1): (3,3),(4,4),... to edge.
Orientation B: missing top-right (elbow bottom-left). Cells: (r,c),(r+1,c),(r+1,c+1). Missing (r,c+1). Line from (r-1,c+2) direction (-1,1).
Orientation C: missing top-left (elbow bottom-right). Cells (r,c+1),(r+1,c),(r+1,c+1). Missing (r,c). Line from (r-1,c-1) direction (-1,-1).
Orientation D: missing bottom-left (elbow top-right). Cells (r,c),(r,c+1),(r+1,c+1). Missing (r+1,c). Line from (r+2,c-1) direction (1,-1).

Place them in different regions so lines are visible. But actually just showing one input yields a gold output; good.

Given the simplicity and that show_transformed_input gives gold output automatically, I'll show 2-3 inputs covering all 4 orientations and multiple objects, then start exam. The student learns from demonstrations. Let me do a couple show_transformed_input calls.

Let me build a 12x12 grid.

Object A at top-left: r=1,c=1: cells (1,1),(1,2),(2,1), missing (2,2). 
Object B at top-right: missing top-right (elbow bottom-left). r=1,c=8: cells (1,8),(2,8),(2,9). Missing (1,9). Line from (0,10) dir (-1,1): only (0,10) then out. Good.
Object C at bottom-left: missing top-left (elbow bottom-right). r=8,c=1: cells (8,2),(9,1),(9,2). Missing (8,1). Line from (7,0) dir(-1,-1): (7,0),(6,-1)out. Just (7,0).
Object D at bottom-right: missing bottom-left (elbow top-right). r=8,c=8: cells (8,8),(8,9),(9,9). Missing (9,8). Line from (10,7) dir(1,-1): (10,7),(11,6) → two cells.

Let me create grid 12x12 all zeros with these cells. Then show_transformed_input.

Actually I want lines to be longer to be clear. Let me choose positions near top-left-ish so diagonals extend far.

Hmm, lines extending might hit other objects; fine, same color.

Let me just make a 12x12 with the four objects as above. The gold output computed by verifier.

Let me instead do two separate demonstrations: one with 2 objects, another with 2 different orientations, to be safe. But each show_transformed_input costs a call; the Student sees gold. Let me do maybe 3 demonstrations to be thorough, covering all orientations and a case with objects sharing.

Actually one input with all four orientations is ideal, showing the rule fully. I'll do one, then maybe a second with a single object oriented differently to reinforce, plus possibly different color.

Let me write grid.

12 rows, 12 cols.

Object A: (1,1),(1,2),(2,1)
Object B: (1,8),(2,8),(2,9)
Object C: (8,2),(9,1),(9,2)
Object D: (8,8),(8,9),(9,9)

color 5.

Let me write rows:
row0: all 0
row1: col1=5,col2=5; col8=5 → [0,5,5,0,0,0,0,0,5,0,0,0]
row2: col1=5; col8=5,col9=5 → [0,5,0,0,0,0,0,0,5,5,0,0]
row3-7: 0
row8: col2=5; col8=5,col9=5 → [0,0,5,0,0,0,0,0,5,5,0,0]
row9: col1=5,col2=5; col9=5 → [0,5,5,0,0,0,0,0,0,5,0,0]
row10,row11: 0

Gold output lines:
A: missing bottom-right (2,2), start (3,3) dir(1,1): (3,3),(4,4),(5,5),(6,6),(7,7),(8,8),(9,9),(10,10),(11,11).
B: missing top-right (1,9), start (0,10) dir(-1,1): (0,10) then out. So just (0,10).
C: missing top-left (8,1), start (7,0) dir(-1,-1): (7,0) then out.
D: missing bottom-left (9,8), start (10,7) dir(1,-1): (10,7),(11,6).

Note A's line passes through (8,8) which is object D's cell — already 5, fine.

Let me call show_transformed_input with this input. It will produce gold and show.

Then maybe a second demo. Actually the rule is simple; student should get it. But to be safe, second demo with single objects and different color and shapes near edges to test boundary. Let me do one more.

Second grid: 8x8, color 2.
Objects:
- orientation B (missing top-right): r=3,c=1: cells (3,1),(4,1),(4,2); missing (3,2); line from (2,3) dir(-1,1): (2,3),(1,4),(0,5).
- orientation D (missing bottom-left): r=1,c=5: cells (1,5),(1,6),(2,6); missing (2,5); line from (3,4) dir(1,-1): (3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1),(7,0).

Grid rows:
row0: 0
row1: col5=2,col6=2 → [0,0,0,0,0,2,2,0]
row2: 0... wait (2,6)=2 → [0,0,0,0,0,0,2,0]
row3: (3,1)=2 → [0,2,0,0,0,0,0,0]
row4: (4,1)=2,(4,2)=2 → [0,2,2,0,0,0,0,0]
others 0.

Hmm but does object B at (3,1),(4,1),(4,2) form correct L? Yes missing top-right (3,2)? 2x2 rows3-4 cols1-2: occupied (3,1),(4,1),(4,2), missing (3,2). Elbow (4,1). Yes.

Let me just do this demo too.

Actually, perhaps one demo is enough. But multiple demos help. Let me do two show_transformed_input calls, then start_exam.

Actually, I should also consider: could there be cases in exam where an L-shape has a different arrangement (not a 2x2 L)? The rule says three of four cells of 2x2. The verifier filters only the four corner-missing cases. Other objects (e.g., 4-cell squares) would produce no filter match and thus not be drawn. But there might be exam inputs with objects that are 2x2 fully? The rule says L-shaped only. Fine.

Let me also consider objects could be adjacent forming bigger components? Verifier uses 4-connectivity and univalued, so two touching L's would merge into one component and no filter match. Probably generator keeps them separate.

Let me issue the two show_transformed_input calls in parallel? They're independent; but I want to ensure correctness. Both use the verifier so fine. I'll call both in one block.

Wait—but the environment might have constraints on input conventions. The verifier just runs. Should be fine.

Let me double check the first input's object extraction with diagonal=F (4-connectivity). Object A cells (1,1),(1,2),(2,1): (1,1)-(1,2) adjacent, (1,1)-(2,1) adjacent. Good. Object B (1,8),(2,8),(2,9): (1,8)-(2,8) adj, (2,8)-(2,9) adj. Good. Object C (8,2),(9,1),(9,2): (9,1)-(9,2) adj, (9,2)-(8,2) adj. Good. Object D (8,8),(8,9),(9,9): (8,8)-(8,9) adj, (8,9)-(9,9) adj. Good.

Great.

Let me now make the calls.
I'll analyze the rule and create demonstration inputs covering all four L orientations.

tools.description: Show the Student a labeled input-output pair that you authored. If your output matches the rule, the pair is shown and you receive a success acknowledgement only. If it does not match, the pair is not shown and you receive the gold output so you can correct it.

tools.description: Probe the student with an input of your choice. You receive the student's predicted output, the gold output, and whether they matched. The student does not see the gold pair unless you later show it with show_example or show_transformed_input.

tools.description: End teaching and send the student to the exam: they must solve held-out generator inputs (unseen in demonstrations or probes) with the history so far. No further teaching after this.

content.text:
Both demonstrations shown. The gold outputs confirm the rule interpretation.

Let me verify first output: A line (3,3),(4,4),(5,5),(6,6),(7,7),(8,8),(9,9),(10,10),(11,11). Output row0 col10=5? That's B's line? Wait B missing top-right at (1,9), start (0,10). Yes output row0 col10=5. Good.

C: missing top-left (8,1), start (7,0) dir(-1,-1) → (7,0). Output row7 col0=5. Good.
D: missing bottom-left (9,8), start (10,7) dir(1,-1): (10,7),(11,6). Output row10 col7=5, row11 col6=5. Yes! row10: [0,0,0,0,0,0,0,5,0,0,5,0] has col7 and col10. Wait col10=5 also — that's A's line (10,10). Yes. And row11 col6=5 and col11=5 (A's (11,11)). Good.

All consistent.

Now the student has seen two demos covering all orientations. I think that's sufficient. Let me start the exam.

Actually, should I query student first to check? Could do a query_student to probe, but not necessary. Given simplicity, start exam. But maybe one probe ensures the student generalizes. However query gives feedback to me but not student. I'll just start exam to save calls. Hmm, but a probe could reveal misunderstanding; but student seems fine with two full demos.

I'll start exam.

Both demonstrations were shown to the Student, covering all four L-orientations (missing corner determines diagonal direction, line starts one step beyond the empty corner and runs to the grid edge in the object's color). The Student now has clear evidence for the rule.
